turn_text: I think the future Prime Minister, Kishida, served in the Abbe cabinet as Foreign Minister. Abbe was the Prime Minister for that time, and I think that I would expect to see an alignment with the free and open Indo-Pacific vision that Prime Minister Abbe did such a great job of articulating. We're leaning into that. I've applauded the Biden administration for its activities to continue focusing on the Quad, to continue focusing on the free and open Indo-Pacific strategy and the vision that Prime Minister Abe so ably laid out years ago. I think that any Prime Minister of Japan is going to continue to want to advance the strength of our alliance and our relationship. Again, the neighborhood is a tough one. And what we'll see with respect to China is an eyes wide open perspective. Japan is looking very carefully at the situation with Taiwan right now. We've all watched Hong Kong, seeing what's happening in Xinjiang with the Uyghur population there. There's a great deal of concern about the posture that China is adopting. From a military standpoint, China has enabled now through a new legislation or a new law their coast guard to be armed and look much more like a military asset. I was in a conversation just today with some of my friends, retired flag officers who were talking me through the fleet of What would they call them ships or amphibious craft that pose a threat to Taiwan that China is building up? under the guise of a commercial fleet, but it has dual use. And if you think about dual use technologies, everybody should be looking at the region in China's maritime posture. I think people are also looking very carefully at what China's been doing in the South China Sea. They've crushed coral reefs, dumped millions of tons of concrete into the ocean. I remember seeing President Xi standing next to then President Obama in the Rose Garden back to 2015, claiming that there was no intention to militarize these islands. Well, any of our listeners that haven't, I encourage them to go Google Firey Cross Reef and take a look at that. This is a military asset with a huge runway, turrets, it's a military asset that's right there in one of the busiest shipping lanes in the world. So we're watching what's happening with China with great concern here in the United States. I can assure you that same level of concern exists in Japan. We also have a huge economic relationship with China. It's a market that's far too large to ignore, but China needs to understand that they have to play by a set of rules that are fair, that are reciprocal, and we cannot tolerate the type of predatory behavior that we've seen coming from China, that I think all of us are aware of whether it be intellectual property theft. the deep subsidization of champion industries that make it impossible or nearly impossible to compete, we need to be pressing back at a return and seeing the China bides by the rule set that market-based economy should be accommodating. With respect to China, I'll turn again to their aggressive posture from a diplomatic standpoint. They continue to focus on organizations like the UN, the World Health Organization, trying to find, you know, you think about standard setting bodies that are multilateral in nature. China has been extraordinarily aggressive in building their presence and building their position and influence. We need to understand that and realize that China's interests are always to looking out for themselves first and foremost. And then from a military standpoint, the buildup that I've seen since my first time in Japan, I think the military budget of China has probably increased eightfold or more. Whereas our posture in the region, I think, is improved. We've got extraordinary capability there. China is ramping up its military capability very, very rapidly. And that is being noticed by every one of our allies in the region, particularly Taiwan, as you would imagine, but Japan is paying very close attention to this as well.
